entries.5245cd274ca2de681c92e45e1119e80058233407: <div sID="gen17681" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Jer.22" sID="Jer.22"/> <div eID="gen17681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17682" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17683" type="x-p"/> Upon occasion of the message sent in the foregoing chapter to the house of the king, we have here recorded some sermons which Jeremiah preached at court, in some preceding reigns, that it might appear they had had fair warning long before that fatal sentence was pronounced upon them, and were put in a way to prevent it. Here is, I. A message sent to the royal family, as it should seem in the reign of Jehoiakim, relating partly to Jehoahaz, who was carried away captive into Egypt, and partly to Jehoiakim, who succeeded him and was now upon the throne. The king and princes are exhorted to execute judgment, and are assured that, if they did so, the royal family should flourish, but otherwise it should be ruined, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.1-Jer.22.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. Jehoahaz, called here Shallum, is lamented, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.10-Jer.22.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. Jehoiakim is reproved and threatened, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.19">ver. 13-19</reference>. II. Another message sent them in the reign of Jehoiachin (alias, Jeconiah) the son of Jehoiakim. He is charged with an obstinate refusal to hear, and is threatened with destruction, and it is foretold that in him Solomon's house should fail, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.20-Jer.22.30">ver. 20-30</reference>.
entries.a5704681a6ff7adac010f6a222c6ac7545ea2cdb: <div eID="gen17683" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17682" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah Preaches before Jehoiakim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen17684" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak there this word, <hi type="super">2</hi> And say, Hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O king of Judah, that sittest upon the throne of David, thou, and thy servants, and thy people that enter in by these gates: <hi type="super">3</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow, neither shed innocent blood in this place. <hi type="super">4</hi> For if ye do this thing indeed, then shall there enter in by the gates of this house kings sitting upon the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, he, and his servants, and his people. <hi type="super">5</hi> But if ye will not hear these words, I swear by myself, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that this house shall become a desolation. <hi type="super">6</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto the king's house of Judah; Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> Gilead unto me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the head of Lebanon: <hi type="italic">yet</hi> surely I will make thee a wilderness, <hi type="italic">and</hi> cities <hi type="italic">which</hi> are not inhabited. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will prepare destroyers against thee, every one with his weapons: and they shall cut down thy choice cedars, and cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> into the fire. <hi type="super">8</hi> And many nations shall pass by this city, and they shall say every man to his neighbour, Wherefore hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> done thus unto this great city? <hi type="super">9</hi> Then they shall answer, Because they have forsaken the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, and worshipped other gods, and served them. <div eID="gen17684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17685" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen17685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17686" type="x-p"/> I. Orders given to Jeremiah to go and preach before the king. In the foregoing chapter we are told that Zedekiah sent messengers to the prophet, but here the prophet is bidden to go, in his own proper person, <hi type="italic">to the house of the king,</hi> and demand his attention to the word of the King of kings (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah!</hi> Subjects must own that where the word of the king is there is power over them, but kings must own that where the word of the Lord is there is power over them. The <hi type="italic">king of Judah</hi> is here spoken to <hi type="italic">as sitting upon the throne of David,</hi> who was a man after God's own heart, as holding his dignity and power by the covenant made with David; let him therefore conform to his example, that he may have the benefit of the promises made to him. With the king his <hi type="italic">servants</hi> are spoken to, because a good government depends upon a good ministry as well as a good king. <div eID="gen17686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17687" type="x-p"/> II. Instructions given him what to preach. <div eID="gen17687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> 1. He must tell them what was their duty, what was the good which the Lord their God required of them, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">v. 3</reference>. They must take care, (1.) That they do all the good they can with the power they have. They must do justice in defence of those that were injured, and must <hi type="italic">deliver the spoiled out of the hand of their oppressors.</hi> This was the duty of their place, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.3">Ps. lxxxii. 3</reference>. Herein they must be ministers of God for good. (2.) That they do no hurt with it, <hi type="italic">no wrong, no violence.</hi> That is the greatest wrong and violence which is done under colour of law and justice, and by those whose business it is to punish and protect from wrong and violence. They must <hi type="italic">do no wrong to the stranger, fatherless, and widow;</hi> for these God does in a particular matter patronise and take under his tuition, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.21-Exod.22.22">Exod. xxii. 21, 22</reference>. <div eID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> 2. He must assure them that the faithful discharge of their duty would advance and secure their prosperity, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.4">v. 4</reference>. There shall then be a succession of kings, an uninterrupted succession, <hi type="italic">upon the throne of David</hi> and of his line, these enjoying a perfect tranquillity, and living in great state and dignity, <hi type="italic">riding in chariots and on horses,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.25">ch. xvii. 25</reference>. Note, the most effectual way to preserve the dignity of the government is to do the duty of it. <div eID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17690" type="x-p"/> 3. He must likewise assure them that the iniquity of their family, if they persisted in it, would be the ruin of their family, though it was a royal family (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">If you will not hear,</hi> will not obey, <hi type="italic">this house shall become a desolation,</hi> the palace of the kings of Judah shall fare no better than other habitations in Jerusalem. Sin has often been the ruin of royal palaces, though ever so stately, ever so strong. This sentence is ratified by an oath: <hi type="italic">I swear by myself</hi> (and God can swear by no greater, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.13">Heb. vi. 13</reference>) that this house shall be laid in ruins. Note, Sin will be the ruin of the houses of princes as well as of mean men. <div eID="gen17690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> 4. He must show how fatal their wickedness would be to their kingdom as well as to themselves, to Jerusalem especially, the royal city, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.6-Jer.22.9">v. 6-9</reference>. (1.) It is confessed that Judah and Jerusalem had been valuable in God's eyes and considerable in their own: <hi type="italic">thou art Gilead unto me and the head of Lebanon.</hi> Their lot was cast in a place that was rich and pleasant as Gilead; Zion was a stronghold, as stately as Lebanon: this they trusted to as their security. But, (2.) This shall not protect them; the country that is now fruitful as Gilead shall be made <hi type="italic">a wilderness.</hi> The cities that are now strong as Lebanon shall be cities <hi type="italic">not inhabited;</hi> and, when the country is laid waste, the cities must be dispeopled. See how easily God's judgments can ruin a nation, and how certainly sin will do it. When this desolating work is to be done, [1.] There shall be those that shall do it effectually (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will prepare destroyers against thee;</hi> I will <hi type="italic">sanctify</hi> them" (so the word is); "I will appoint them to this service and use them in it." Note, When destruction is designed destroyers are prepared, and perhaps are in the preparing, and things are working towards the designed destruction, and are getting ready for it, long before. And who can contend with destroyers of God's preparing? They shall destroy cities as easily as men fell trees in a forest: <hi type="italic">They shall cut down thy choice cedars;</hi> and yet, when they are down, shall value them no more than thorns and briers; they shall <hi type="italic">cast them into the fire,</hi> for their choicest cedars have become rotten ones and good for nothing else. [2.] There shall be those who shall be ready to justify God in the doing of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.8-Jer.22.9">v. 8, 9</reference>); persons of <hi type="italic">many nations,</hi> when they <hi type="italic">pass by</hi> the ruins of <hi type="italic">this city</hi> in their travels, will ask, "<hi type="italic">Wherefore hath the Lord done thus unto this city?</hi> How came so strong a city to be overpowered? so rich a city to be impoverished? so populous a city to be depopulated? so holy a city to be profaned? and a city that had been so dear to God to be abandoned by him?" The reason is so obvious that it shall be ready in every man's mouth. Ask those <hi type="italic">that go by the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.29">Job xxi. 29</reference>. Ask the next man you meet, and he will tell you it was because they changed their gods, which other nations never used to do. They forsook <hi type="italic">the covenant</hi> of Jehovah their own God, revolted from their allegiance to him and from the duty which their covenant with him bound them to, and they <hi type="italic">worshipped other gods and served them,</hi> in contempt of him; and therefore he gave them up to this destruction. Note, God never casts any off until they first cast him off. "Go," says God to the prophet, "and preach this to the royal family."
entries.e7867227a724601bd71978953c46efbe2a8057b6: <div eID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Shallum and Jehoiakim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen17692" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: <hi type="italic">but</hi> weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country. <hi type="super">11</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> touching Shallum the son of Josiah king of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father, which went forth out of this place; He shall not return thither any more: <hi type="super">12</hi> But he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive, and shall see this land no more. <hi type="super">13</hi> Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; <hi type="italic">that</hi> useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work; <hi type="super">14</hi> That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and <hi type="italic">it is</hi> cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion. <hi type="super">15</hi> Shalt thou reign, because thou closest <hi type="italic">thyself</hi> in cedar? did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">it was</hi> well with him? <hi type="super">16</hi> He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then <hi type="italic">it was</hi> well <hi type="italic">with him: was</hi> not this to know me? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> But thine eyes and thine heart <hi type="italic">are</hi> not but for thy covetousness, and for to shed innocent blood, and for oppression, and for violence, to do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah; They shall not lament for him, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Ah my brother! or, Ah sister! they shall not lament for him, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Ah lord! or, Ah his glory! <hi type="super">19</hi> He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen17692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> Kings, though they are gods to us, are men to God, and shall <hi type="italic">die like men;</hi> so it appears in these verses, where we have a sentence of death passed upon two kings who reigned successively in Jerusalem, two brothers, and both the ungracious sons of a very pious father. <div eID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17694" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the doom of Shallum, who doubtless is the same with Jehoahaz, for he is that son of Josiah king of Judah who reigned <hi type="italic">in the stead of Josiah his father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.11">v. 11</reference>), which Jehoahaz did by the act of the people, who made him king though he was not the eldest son, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.30">2 Kings xxiii. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.1">2 Chron. xxxvi. 1</reference>. Among the sons of Josiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.3.15">1 Chron. iii. 15</reference>) there is one Shallum mentioned, and not Jehoahaz. Perhaps the people preferred him before his elder brother because they thought him a more active daring young man, and fitter to rule; but God soon showed them the folly of their injustice, and that it could not prosper, for within three months the king of Egypt came upon him, deposed him, and carried him away prisoner into Egypt, as God had threatened, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">Deut. xxviii. 68</reference>. It does not appear that any of the people were taken into captivity with him. We have the story <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.34">2 Kings xxiii. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.4">2 Chron. xxxvi. 4</reference>. Now here, 1. The people are directed to lament him rather than his father Josiah: "<hi type="italic">Weep not for the dead,</hi> weep not any more for Josiah." Jeremiah had been himself a true mourner for him, and had stirred up the people to mourn for him (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2 Chron. xxxv. 25</reference>): yet now he will have them go out of mourning for him, though it was but three months after his death, and to turn their tears into another channel. They must weep sorely for Jehoahaz, who had gone into Egypt; not that there was any great loss of him to the public, as there was of his father, but that his case was much more deplorable. Josiah went to the grave in peace and honour, was prevented from seeing the evil to come in this world and removed to see the good to come in the other world; and therefore, <hi type="italic">Weep not for him,</hi> but for his unhappy son, who is likely to live and die in disgrace and misery, a wretched captive. Note, Dying saints may be justly envied, while living sinners are justly pitied. And so dismal perhaps the prospect of the times may be that tears even for a Josiah, even for a Jesus, must be restrained, that they may be reserved for <hi type="italic">ourselves and for our children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.28">Luke xxiii. 28</reference>. 2. The reason given is because he shall never return out of captivity, as he and his people expected, but shall die there. They were loth to believe this, therefore it is repeated here again and again, He shall <hi type="italic">return no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.10">v. 10</reference>. He shall never have the pleasure of seeing <hi type="italic">his native country,</hi> but shall have the continual grief of hearing of the desolations of it. He has gone <hi type="italic">forth out of this place,</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">never return,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall die in the place whither they have led him captive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.12">v. 12</reference>. This came of his forsaking the good example of his father, and usurping the right of his elder brother. In Ezekiel's lamentation for the princes of Israel this Jehoahaz is represented as a young lion, that soon learned to <hi type="italic">catch the prey,</hi> but was taken, and brought in chains to Egypt, and was long expected to return, but in vain. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.3-Ezek.19.5">Ezek. xix. 3-5</reference>. <div eID="gen17694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the doom of Jehoiakim, who succeeded him. Whether he had any better right to the crown than Shallum we know not; for, though he was older than his predecessor, there seems to be another son of Josiah, older than he, called <hi type="italic">Johanan,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.15">1 Chron. iii. 15</reference>. But this we know he ruled no better, and fared no better at last. Here we have, <div eID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17696" type="x-p"/> 1. His sins faithfully reproved. It is not fit for a private person to say to a king, <hi type="italic">Thou art wicked;</hi> but a prophet, who has a message from God, betrays his trust if he does not deliver it, be it ever so unpleasing, even to kings themselves. Jehoiakim is not here charged with idolatry, and probably he had not yet put Urijah the prophet to death (as we find afterwards he did, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.22-Jer.26.23">ch. xxvi. 22, 23</reference>), for then he would have been told of it here; but the crimes for which he is here reproved are, (1.) Pride and affection of pomp and splendour; as if all the business of a king were to look great, and to do good were to be the least of his care. He must build himself a stately palace, a <hi type="italic">wide house,</hi> and <hi type="italic">large chambers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.14">v. 14</reference>. He must have <hi type="italic">windows cut out</hi> after the newest fashion, perhaps like sash-windows with us. The rooms must be <hi type="italic">ceiled with cedar,</hi> the richest sort of wood. His house must be as well-roofed and wainscoted as the temple itself, or else it will not please him, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.15-1Kgs.6.16">1 Kings vi. 15, 16</reference>. Nay, it must exceed that, for it must be painted with <hi type="italic">minium,</hi> or <hi type="italic">vermilion,</hi> which dyes red, or, as some read it, with <hi type="italic">indigo,</hi> which dyes blue. No doubt it is lawful for princes and great men to build, and beautify, and furnish their houses so as is agreeable to their dignity; but he that knows what is in man knew that Jehoiakim did this in the pride of his heart, which makes that to be sinful, exceedingly sinful, which is in itself lawful. Those therefore that are enlarging their houses, and making them more sumptuous, have need to look well to the frame of their own spirits in the doing of it, and carefully to watch against all the workings of vain-glory. But that which was particularly amiss in Jehoiakim's case was that he did this when he could not but perceive, both by the word of God and by his providence, that divine judgments were breaking in upon him. He reigned his first three years by the permission and allowance of the king of Egypt, and all the rest by the permission and allowance of the king of Babylon; and yet he that was no better than a viceroy will covet to vie with the greatest monarchs in building and furniture. Observe how peremptory he is in this resolution: "<hi type="italic">I will build myself a wide house;</hi> I am resolved <hi type="italic">I will,</hi> whoever advises me to the contrary." Note, It is the common folly of those that are sinking in their estates to covet to make a fair show. Many have unhumbled hearts under humbling providences, and look most haughty when God is bringing them down. This is striving with our Maker. (2.) Carnal security and confidence in his wealth, depending upon the continuance of his prosperity, as if his mountain now stood so strong that it could never be moved. He thought he must reign without any disturbance or interruption because he had <hi type="italic">enclosed himself in cedar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">v. 15</reference>), as if that were too fine to be assaulted and too strong to be broken through, and as if God himself could not, for pity, give up such a stately house as that to be burned. Thus when Christ spoke of the destruction of the temple his disciples came to him, to show him what a magnificent structure it was, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Matt. xxiii. 38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.1">xxiv. 1</reference>. Note, Those wretchedly deceive themselves who think their present prosperity is a lasting security, and dream of reigning because they are <hi type="italic">enclosed in cedar.</hi> It is but in his own conceit that <hi type="italic">the rich man's wealth is his strong city.</hi> (3.) Some think he is here charged with sacrilege, and robbing the house of God to beautify and adorn his own house. He <hi type="italic">cuts him out</hi> my <hi type="italic">windows</hi> (so it is in the margin), which some understand as if he had taken windows out of the temple to put into his own palace and then <hi type="italic">painted them</hi> (as it follows) <hi type="italic">with vermilion,</hi> that it might not be discovered, but might look of a piece with his own buildings. Note, Those cheat themselves, and ruin themselves at last, who think to enrich themselves by robbing God and his house; and, however they may disguise it, God discovers it. (4.) He is here charged with extortion and oppression, violence and injustice. He <hi type="italic">built his house by unrighteousness,</hi> with money unjustly got and materials which were not honestly come by, and perhaps upon ground obtained as Ahab obtained Naboth's vineyard. And, because he went beyond what he could afford, he defrauded his workmen of their wages, which is one of the sins that <hi type="italic">cries in the ears of the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 4</reference>. God takes notice of the wrong done by the greatest of men to their poor servants and labourers, and will repay those, in justice, that will not in justice pay those whom they employ, but <hi type="italic">use their neighbour's service without wages.</hi> Observe, The greatest of men must look upon the meanest as their neighbours, and be just to them accordingly, and love them as themselves. Jehoiakim was oppressive, not only in his buildings, but in the administration of his government. He did not do justice, made no conscience of shedding innocent blood, when it was to serve the purposes of his ambition, avarice, and revenge. He was all for <hi type="italic">oppression</hi> and <hi type="italic">violence,</hi> not to threaten it only, but to do it; and, when he was set upon any act of injustice, nothing should stop him, but he would go through with it. And that which was at the bottom of all was covetousness, that love of <hi type="italic">money which is the root of all evil. Thy eyes and thy heart are not but for covetousness;</hi> they were for that, and nothing else. Observe, In covetousness the heart walks after the eyes: it is therefore called <hi type="italic">the lust of the eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.16">1 John ii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job xxxi. 7</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">setting the eyes upon that which is not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. The eyes and the heart are then for covetousness when the aims and affections are wholly set upon the wealth of this world; and, where they are so, the temptation is strong to murder, oppression, and all manner of violence and villany. (5.) That which aggravated all his sins was that he was the son of a good father, who had left him a good example, if he would but have followed it (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Did not thy father eat and drink?</hi> When Jehoiakim enlarged and enlightened his house it is probable that he spoke scornfully of his father for contenting himself with such a mean and inconvenient dwelling, below the grandeur of a sovereign prince, and ridiculed him as one that had a dull fancy, a low spirit, and could not find in his heart to lay out his money, nor cared for what was fashionable; that should not serve him which served his father: but God, by the prophet, tells him that his father, though he had not the spirit of building, was a man of an excellent spirit, a better man than he, and did better for himself and his family. Those children that despise their parents' old fashions commonly come short of their real excellences. Jeremiah tells him, [1.] That he was directed to do his duty by his father's practice: He <hi type="italic">did judgment and justice;</hi> he never did wrong to any of his subjects, never oppressed them, nor put any hardship upon them, but was careful to preserve all their just rights and properties. Nay, he not only did not abuse his power for the support of wrong, but he used it for the maintaining of right. He <hi type="italic">judged the cause of the poor and needy,</hi> was ready to hear the cause of the meanest of his subjects and do them justice. Note, The care of magistrates must be, not to support their grandeur and take their ease, but to do good, not only not to oppress the poor themselves, but to defend those that are oppressed. [2.] That he was encouraged to do his duty by his father's prosperity. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God accepted him: "<hi type="italic">Was not this to know me, saith the Lord?</hi> Did he not hereby make it to appear that he rightly knew his God, and worshipped him, and consequently was known and owned of him?" Note, The right knowledge of God consists in doing our duty, particularly that which is the duty of our place and station in the world. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He himself had the comfort of it: <hi type="italic">Did he not eat and drink</hi> soberly and cheerfully, so as to fit himself for his business, <hi type="italic">for strength and not for drunkenness?</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.17">Eccl. x. 17</reference>. He did <hi type="italic">eat, and drink, and do judgment;</hi> he did not (as perhaps Jehoiakim and his princes did) <hi type="italic">drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of the afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Prov. xxxi. 5</reference>. He did <hi type="italic">eat and drink;</hi> that is, God blessed him with great plenty, and he had the comfortable enjoyment of it himself and gave handsome entertainments to his friends, was very hospitable and very charitable. It was Jehoiakim's pride that he had built a fine house, but Josiah's true praise that he kept a good house. Many times those have least in them of true generosity that have the greatest affection for pomp and grandeur; for, to support the extravagant expense of that, hospitality, bounty to the poor, yea, and justice itself, will be pinched. It is better to live with Josiah in an old-fashioned house, and do good, than live with Jehoiakim in a stately house, and leave debts unpaid. Josiah did <hi type="italic">justice and judgment,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">it was well with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">v. 15</reference>, and it is repeated again, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">v. 16</reference>. He lived very comfortably; his own subjects, and all his neighbours, respected him; and whatever he put his hand to prospered. Note, While we do well we may expect it will be well with us. This Jehoiakim knew, that his father found the way of duty to be the way of comfort, and yet he would not tread in his steps. Note, It should engage us to keep up religion in our day that our godly parents kept it up in theirs and recommended it to us from their own experience of the benefit of it. They told us that they had found the promises which godliness has of the <hi type="italic">life that now</hi> is made good to them, and that religion and piety are friendly to outward prosperity. So that we are inexcusable if we turn aside from that good way. <div eID="gen17696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17697" type="x-p"/> 2. Here we have Jehoiakim's doom faithfully read, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18-Jer.22.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. We may suppose that it was in the utmost peril of his own life that Jeremiah here foretold the shameful death of Jehoiakim; but <hi type="italic">thus saith the Lord concerning</hi> him, and therefore thus saith he. (1.) He shall die unlamented; he shall make himself so odious by his oppression and cruelty that all about him shall be glad to part with him, and none shall do him the honour of dropping one tear for him, whereas his father, who <hi type="italic">did judgment and justice,</hi> was universally lamented; and it is promised to Zedekiah that he should be lamented at his death, for he conducted himself better than Jehoiakim had done, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">ch. xxxiv. 5</reference>. His relations shall not <hi type="italic">lament him,</hi> no, not with the common expressions of grief used at the funeral of the meanest, where they cried, <hi type="italic">Ah, my brother!</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Ah, sister!</hi> His subjects shall not lament him, nor cry out, as they used to do at the graves of their princes, <hi type="italic">Ah, lord!</hi> or <hi type="italic">Ah his glory!</hi> It is sad for any to live so that, when they die, none will be sorry to part with them. Nay, (2.) He shall lie unburied. This is worse than the former. Even those that have no tears to grace the funerals of the dead with would willingly have them buried out of their sight; but Jehoiakim shall be <hi type="italic">buried with the burial of an ass,</hi> that is, he shall have no burial at all, but his dead body shall be cast into a ditch or upon a dunghill; it shall be <hi type="italic">drawn,</hi> or dragged, ignominiously, and <hi type="italic">cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.</hi> It is said, in the story of Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2 Chron. xxxvi. 6</reference>), that Nebuchadnezzar <hi type="italic">bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ezek.19.9">Ezek. xix. 9</reference>) that he was <hi type="italic">brought in chains to the king of Babylon.</hi> But it is probable that he died a prisoner, before he was carried away to Babylon as was intended; perhaps he died for grief, or, in the pride of his heart, hastened his own end, and, for that reason, was denied a decent burial, as self-murderers usually are with us. Josephus says that Nebuchadnezzar slew him at Jerusalem, and left his body thus exposed, somewhere at a great distance from the <hi type="italic">gates of Jerusalem.</hi> And it is said (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.6">2 Kings xxiv. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">he slept with his fathers.</hi> When he built himself a stately house, no doubt he designed himself a stately sepulchre; but see how he was disappointed. Note, Those that are lifted up with great pride are commonly reserved for some great disgrace in life or death.
entries.320f8afdf1516308beb76972a18b89a941b37ffa: <div eID="gen17697" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Judah; The Doom of Jeconiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen17698" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Go up to Lebanon, and cry; and lift up thy voice in Bashan, and cry from the passages: for all thy lovers are destroyed. <hi type="super">21</hi> I spake unto thee in thy prosperity; <hi type="italic">but</hi> thou saidst, I will not hear. This <hi type="italic">hath been</hi> thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice. <hi type="super">22</hi> The wind shall eat up all thy pastors, and thy lovers shall go into captivity: surely then shalt thou be ashamed and confounded for all thy wickedness. <hi type="super">23</hi> O inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars, how gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee, the pain as of a woman in travail! <hi type="super">24</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> I live, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence; <hi type="super">25</hi> And I will give thee into the hand of them that seek thy life, and into the hand <hi type="italic">of them</hi> whose face thou fearest, even into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of the Chaldeans. <hi type="super">26</hi> And I will cast thee out, and thy mother that bare thee, into another country, where ye were not born; and there shall ye die. <hi type="super">27</hi> But to the land whereunto they desire to return, thither shall they not return. <hi type="super">28</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> this man Coniah a despised broken idol? <hi type="italic">is he</hi> a vessel wherein <hi type="italic">is</hi> no pleasure? wherefore are they cast out, he and his seed, and are cast into a land which they know not? <hi type="super">29</hi> O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">30</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Write ye this man childless, a man <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah. <div eID="gen17698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17699" type="x-p"/> This prophecy seems to have been calculated for the ungracious inglorious reign of Jeconiah, or Jehoiachin, the son of Jehoiakim, who succeeded him in the government, reigned but three months, and was then carried captive to Babylon, where he lived many years, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31">ch. lii. 31</reference>. We have, in these verses, a prophecy, <div eID="gen17699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17700" type="x-p"/> I. Of the desolations of the kingdom, which were now hastening on apace, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.20-Jer.22.23">v. 20-23</reference>. Jerusalem and Judah are here spoken to, or the Jewish state as a single person, and we have it here under a threefold character:—1. Very haughty in a day of peace and safety (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I spoke unto thee in thy prosperity,</hi> spoke by my servants the prophets, reproofs, admonitions, counsels, <hi type="italic">but thou saidst, I will not hear,</hi> I will not heed, <hi type="italic">thou obeyedst not my voice,</hi> and wast resolved that thou wouldst not, and hadst the front to tell me so." It is common for those that live at ease to live in contempt of the word of God. <hi type="italic">Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked.</hi> This is so much the worse that they had it by kind: <hi type="italic">This has been thy manner from thy youth.</hi> They were called <hi type="italic">transgressors from the womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>. 2. Very timorous upon the alarms of trouble (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.20">v. 20</reference>): "When thou seest <hi type="italic">all thy lovers destroyed,</hi> when thou findest thy idols unable to help thee and thy foreign alliances failing thee, thou wilt then go up to Lebanon, and cry, as one undone and giving up all for lost, cry with a bitter cry; thou wilt cry, <hi type="italic">Help, help, or we are lost;</hi> thou wilt <hi type="italic">lift up thy voice</hi> in fearful shrieks upon <hi type="italic">Lebanon and Bashan,</hi> two high hills, in hope to be heard thence by the advantage of the rising ground. Thou wilt <hi type="italic">cry from the passages,</hi> from the roads, where thou wilt ever and anon be in distress." Thou wilt cry from <hi type="italic">Abarim</hi> (so some read it, as a proper name), a famous mountain in the border of Moab. "Thou wilt cry, as those that are in great consternation use to do, to all about thee; but in vain, for (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.22">v. 22</reference>) <hi type="italic">the wind shall eat up all thy pastors,</hi> or <hi type="italic">rulers,</hi> that should protect and lead thee, and provide for thy safety; they shall be blasted, and withered, and brought to nothing, as buds and blossoms are by a bleak or freezing wind; they shall be devoured suddenly, insensibly, and irresistibly, as fruits by the wind. <hi type="italic">Thy lovers,</hi> that thou dependest upon and hast an affection for, shall <hi type="italic">go into captivity,</hi> and shall be so far from saving thee that they shall not be able to save themselves." 3. Very tame under the heavy and lasting pressures of trouble: "When there appears no relief from any of thy confederates, and thy own priests are at a loss, <hi type="italic">then shalt thou be ashamed and confounded for all thy wickedness,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.22.22">v. 22</reference>. Note, Many will never be ashamed of their sins till they are brought by them to the last extremity; and it is well if we get this good by our straits to be brought by them to confusion for our sins. The Jewish state is here called <hi type="italic">an inhabitant of Lebanon,</hi> because that famous forest was within their border (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.23">v. 23</reference>), and all their country was wealthy, and well-guarded as with Lebanon's natural fastnesses; but so proud and haughty were they that they are said to <hi type="italic">make their nest in the cedars,</hi> where they thought themselves out of the reach of all danger, and whence they looked with contempt upon all about them. "But, <hi type="italic">how gracious wilt thou be when pangs come upon thee!</hi> Then thou wilt humble thyself before God and promise amendment. When thou art overthrown in stony places thou wilt be glad to <hi type="italic">hear those words</hi> which in thy prosperity <hi type="italic">thou wouldst not hear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.141.6">Ps. cxli. 6</reference>. Then thou wilt endeavour to make thyself acceptable with that God whom, before, thou madest light of." Note, Many have their pangs of piety who, when the pangs are over, show that they have no true piety. Some give another sense of it: "What will all thy pomp, and state, and wealth avail thee? What will become of it all, or what comfort shalt thou have of it, when thou shalt be in these distresses? No more than <hi type="italic">a woman in travail,</hi> full of pains and fears, can take comfort in her ornaments while she is in that condition." So Mr. Gataker. Note, Those that are proud of their worldly advantages would do well to consider how they will look when pangs come upon them, and how they will then have lost all their beauty. <div eID="gen17700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a prophecy of the disgrace of the king; his name was <hi type="italic">Jeconiah,</hi> but he is here once and again called <hi type="italic">Coniah,</hi> in contempt. The prophet shortens or nicks his name, and gives him, as we say, a nickname, perhaps to denote that he should be despoiled of his dignity, that his reign should be shortened, and the number of his months cut off in the midst. Two instances of dishonour are here put upon him:— <div eID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall be carried away <hi type="italic">into captivity</hi> and shall spend and end his days in bondage. He was born to a crown, but it should quickly fall from his head, and he should exchange it for fetters. Observe the steps of this judgment. (1.) God will abandon him, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">v. 24</reference>. The God of truth says it, and confirms it with an oath: "<hi type="italic">Though he were the signet upon my right hand</hi> (his predecessors have been so, and he might have been so if he had conducted himself well, but he being degenerated) <hi type="italic">I will pluck him thence.</hi>" The godly kings of Judah had been as signets on God's right hand, near and dear to him; he had gloried in them, and made use of them as instruments of his government, as the prince does of his signet-ring, or sign manual; but Coniah has made himself utterly unworthy of the honour, and therefore the privilege of his birth shall be no security to him; notwithstanding that, he shall be thrown off. Answerable to this threatening against Jeconiah is God's promise to Zerubbabel, when he made him his people's guide in their return out of captivity (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.23">Hag. ii. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will take thee, O Zerubbabel! my servant, and make thee as a signet.</hi> Those that think themselves as signets on God's right hand must not be secure, but fear lest they be plucked thence. (2.) The king of Babylon shall seize him. <hi type="italic">Those</hi> know not what enemies and mischiefs they lie exposed to who have thrown themselves out of God's protection, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.25">v. 25</reference>. The Chaldeans are here said to be such as had a spite to <hi type="italic">Coniah;</hi> they <hi type="italic">sought his life;</hi> no less than that, they thought, would satisfy their rage; they were such as he had a dread of (they are those <hi type="italic">whose face thou fearest</hi>) which would make it the more terrible to him to fall into their hands, especially when it was God himself that gave <hi type="italic">him into their hands.</hi> And, if God deliver him to them, who can deliver him from them? (3.) He and his family shall be carried to Babylon, where they shall wear out many tedious years of their lives in a miserable captivity—<hi type="italic">he and his mother</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.26">v. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">he and his seed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">v. 28</reference>), that is, he and all the royal family (for he had no children of his own when he went into captivity), or he and the children in his loins; they shall all be cast out to another country, to a strange country, <hi type="italic">a country where they were not born,</hi> nor such a country as that where they were born, <hi type="italic">a land which they know not,</hi> in which they have no acquaintance with whom to converse or from whom to expect any kindness. Thither they shall be carried, from a land where they were entitled to dominion, into a land where they shall be compelled to servitude. But have they no hopes of seeing their own country again? No: <hi type="italic">To the land whereunto they desire to return, thither shall they not return,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.27">v. 27</reference>. They conducted themselves ill in it when they were in it, and therefore they shall never see it more. Jehoahaz was carried to Egypt, the land of the south, Jeconiah to Babylon, the land of the north, both far remote, the quite contrary way, and must never expect to meet again, nor either of them to breathe their native air again. Those that had abused the dominion they had over others were justly brought thus under the dominion of others. Those that had indulged and gratified their sinful desires, by their oppression, luxury, and cruelty, were justly denied the gratification of their innocent desire to see their own native country again. We may observe something very emphatic in that part of this threatening (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.26">v. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">In the country where you were not born, there shall you die.</hi> As there is a <hi type="italic">time to be born</hi> and a <hi type="italic">time to die,</hi> so there is a place to be born in and a place to die in. We know where we were born, but where we shall die we know not; it is enough that our God knows. Let it be our care that we die in Christ, and then it will be well with us, wherever we die, though it should be in a far country. (4.) This shall render him very mean and despicable in the eyes of all his neighbours. They shall be ready to say (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">v. 28</reference>), "<hi type="italic">This is Coniah a despised broken idol?</hi> Yes, certainly he is, and much debased from what he was." [1.] Time was when he was dignified, nay, when he was almost deified. The people who had seen his father lately deposed were ready to adore him when they saw him upon the throne, but now <hi type="italic">he is a despised broken idol,</hi> which, when it was whole, was worshipped, but, when it is rotten and broken, is thrown by and despised, and nobody regards it, or remembers what it has been. Note, What is idolized will, first or last, be despised and broken; what is unjustly honoured will be justly contemned, and rivals with God will be the scorn of man. Whatever we idolize we shall be disappointed in and then shall despise. [2.] Time was when he was delighted in; but now he is <hi type="italic">a vessel in which is not pleasure,</hi> or to which there is no desire, either because grown out of fashion or because cracked or dirtied, and so rendered unserviceable. Those whom God has no pleasure in will, some time or other, be so mortified that men will have no pleasure in them. <div eID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17703" type="x-p"/> 2. He shall leave no posterity to inherit his honour. The prediction of this is ushered in with a solemn preface (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">O earth, earth, earth! hear the word of the Lord.</hi> Let all the inhabitants of the world take notice of these judgments of God upon a nation and a family that had been near and dear to him, and thence infer that God is impartial in the administration of justice. Or it is an appeal to the earth itself on which we tread, since those that dwell on earth are so deaf and careless, like that (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa. i. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hear, O heavens! and give ear, O earth!</hi> God's word, however slighted, will be heard; the earth itself will be made to hear it, and yield to it, when it, and all the works that are therein, shall be burnt up. Or it is a call to men that <hi type="italic">mind earthly things,</hi> that are swallowed up in those things and are inordinate in the pursuit of them; such have need to be called upon again and again, and a third time, to <hi type="italic">hear the word of the Lord.</hi> Or it is a call to men considered as mortal, of the earth, and hastening to the earth again. We all are so; earth we are, <hi type="italic">dust we are,</hi> and, in consideration of that, are concerned to hear and regard <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord,</hi> that, though we are earth, we may be found among those whose names are written in heaven. Now that which is here to be taken notice of is that Jeconiah is <hi type="italic">written childless</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.30">v. 30</reference>), that is, as it follows, <hi type="italic">No man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David.</hi> In him the line of David was extinct as a royal line. Some think that he had children born in Babylon because mention is made of his seed being cast out there (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">v. 28</reference>) and that they died before him. We read in the genealogy (<reference osisRef="1Chr.3.17">1 Chron. iii. 17</reference>) of seven sons of Jeconiah Assir (that is, Jeconiah the captive) of whom Salathiel is the first. Some think that they were only his adopted sons, and that when it is said (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.12">Matt. i. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Jeconiah begat Salathiel,</hi> no more is meant than that he bequeathed to him what claims and pretensions he had to the government, the rather because Salathiel is called the <hi type="italic">son of Neri</hi> of <hi type="italic">the house of Nathan,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.27">Luke iii. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.31">31</reference>. Whether he had children begotten, or only adopted, thus far he was childless that none of his seed ruled as kings in Judah. He was the <hi type="italic">Augustulus</hi> of that empire, in whom it determined. Whoever are childless, it is God that writes them so; and those who take no care to do good in their days cannot expect to prosper in their days.  <chapter eID="Jer.22"/> <div eID="gen17703" type="x-p"/>

entries.9fbc5bc4c5485658723b709e85875747e124b2b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10051"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.22.1-Jer.22.30">Jr 22:1-30</reference>. Exhortation to Repentance; Judgment on Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah.</title> <div sID="gen17913" type="x-p"/> Belonging to an earlier period than the twenty-first chapter, namely, the reigns of Shallum or Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.10">Jr 22:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.20">13, 20</reference>). Jeremiah often groups his prophecies, not by chronological order, but by similarity of subjects; thus <reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jr 22:3</reference> corresponds to <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>. Grotius thinks that Jeremiah here repeats to Zedekiah what he had announced to that king's predecessors formerly (namely, his brother and brother's son), of a similar bearing, and which had since come to pass; a warning to Zedekiah. Probably, in arranging his prophecies they were grouped for the first time in the present order, designed by the Holy Spirit to set forth the series of kings of Judah, all four alike, failing in "righteousness," followed at last by the "King," a righteous Branch raised unto David, in the house of Judah, "the Lord our righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>). The unrighteousness of Zedekiah suggested the review of his predecessors' failure in the same respects, and consequent punishment, which ought to have warned him, but did not.<div eID="gen17913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10051"/><hi type="bold">1. Go down--</hi>The temple (where Jeremiah had been prophesying) was higher than the king's palace on Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">Jr 36:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.20">2Ch 23:20</reference>). Hence the phrase, "Go down."<div eID="gen17914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king of Judah--</hi>perhaps including each of the four successive kings, to whom it was consecutively addressed, here brought together in one picture: Shallum, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.11">Jr 22:11</reference>; Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.18">Jr 22:13-18</reference>; Jeconiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jr 22:24</reference>; Zedekiah, the address to whom (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">11, 12</reference>) suggests notice of the rest. <div eID="gen17915" type="x-p"/>
entries.815d24b3e5b51b7de54daf465951221a4c8bbbe4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10052"/><div sID="gen17916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10052"/><hi type="bold">2. these gates--</hi>of the king's palace. <div eID="gen17916" type="x-p"/>
entries.2819f274cece20f5b1f8b539b4241ab292dbc236: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10053"/><div sID="gen17917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10053"/>3. Jehoiakim is meant here especially: he, by oppression, levied the tribute imposed on him by Pharaoh-necho, king of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.3">2Ch 36:3</reference>), and taxed his people, and took their labor without pay, to build gorgeous palaces for himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.17">Jr 22:13-17</reference>), and shed innocent blood, for example, that of Urijah the prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.20-Jer.26.24">Jr 26:20-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.35">2Ki 23:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">24:4</reference>). <div eID="gen17917" type="x-p"/>
entries.8729beba796a3ddbaf4c1eb03767e77e3ad5c7ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10054"/><div sID="gen17918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10054"/><hi type="bold">4. upon the throne of David--</hi>literally, "or David on his throne" (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">Jr 13:13</reference>). This verse is repeated substantially from <reference osisRef="Jer.17.25">Jr 17:25</reference>.<div eID="gen17918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his servants--</hi>so the Keri. But Chetib, singular, "his servant;" that is, distributively, "each with his servants;" <reference osisRef="Jer.17.25">Jr 17:25</reference>, "their princes." <div eID="gen17919" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1990f57dddc0d3001ff774abe25a9e916e18ab6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10055"/><div sID="gen17920" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10055"/><hi type="bold">5. I swear by myself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.6.13">He 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17">17</reference>). God swears because it seemed to them incredible that the family of David should be cast off.<div eID="gen17920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this house--</hi>the king's, where Jeremiah spake (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.4">Jr 22:4</reference>). <div eID="gen17921" type="x-p"/>
entries.2446c8ba7180a05d1f9f825259fa4c21717a769f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10056"/><div sID="gen17922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10056"/>6. Though thou art as beautiful as Gilead, and as majestic in Mine eyes (before Me) as the summit of Lebanon, yet surely (the Hebrew is a formula of swearing to express certainly: "If I do not make thee ... believe Me not ever hereafter": so "as truly as I live," <reference osisRef="Num.14.28">Nu 14:28</reference>; "surely," <reference osisRef="Num.14.35">Nu 14:35</reference>). The mention of Gilead may allude not only to its past beauty, but covertly also to its desolation by the judgment on Israel; a warning now to Judah and the house of David. "Lebanon" is appropriately mentioned, as the king's house was built of its noble cedars.<div eID="gen17922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cities--</hi>not other cities, but the different parts of the city of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.27">2Sa 12:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.25">2Ki 10:25</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen17923" type="x-p"/>
entries.14b5bd9a151f6bb73dd143df4fe0e1f201067099: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10057"/><div sID="gen17924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10057"/><hi type="bold">7. prepare--</hi>literally, "sanctify," or solemnly set apart for a particular work (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy choice cedars--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Is 37:24</reference>). Thy palaces built of choice cedars (<reference osisRef="Song.1.17">So 1:17</reference>). <div eID="gen17925" type="x-p"/>
entries.581ecf4297b262e91a1b6788c1774eaff4d0b6e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10058"/><div sID="gen17926" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10058"/>8. (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">De 29:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.25">25</reference>). The Gentile nations, more intelligent than you, shall understand that which ye do not, namely, that this city is a spectacle of God's vengeance [Calvin]. <div eID="gen17926" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a84cff82ed876966a37dff27f9dd79a7008baa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10059"/><div sID="gen17927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10059"/>9. (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.17">2Ki 22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen17927" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfbf80c41153bfaf4cb86023c7b7e4d4f6473b47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10060"/><div sID="gen17928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10060"/><hi type="bold">10-11. Weep ... not for--</hi>that is, not so much for Josiah, who was taken away by death from the evil to come (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.20">2Ki 22:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Is 57:1</reference>); as for Shallum or Jehoahaz, his son (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.30">2Ki 23:30</reference>), who, after a three months' reign, was carried off by Pharaoh-necho into Egypt, never to see his native land again (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31-2Kgs.23.34">2Ki 23:31-34</reference>). Dying saints are justly to be envied, while living sinners are to be pitied. The allusion is to the great weeping of the people at the death of Josiah, and on each anniversary of it, in which Jeremiah himself took a prominent part (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.24">2Ch 35:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">25</reference>). The name "Shallum" is here given in irony to Jehoahaz, who reigned but three months; as if he were a second Shallum, son of Jabesh, who reigned only one month in Samaria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.13">2Ki 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.1-2Chr.36.4">2Ch 36:1-4</reference>). Shallum means "retribution," a name of no good omen to him [Grotius]; originally the people called him Shallom, indicative of peace and prosperity. But Jeremiah applies it in irony. <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.15">1Ch 3:15</reference>, calls Shallum the fourth son of Josiah. The people raised him to the throne before his brother Eliakim or Jehoiakim, though the latter was the older (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31">2Ki 23:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.1">2Ch 36:1</reference>); perhaps on account of Jehoiakim's extravagance (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">15</reference>). Jehoiakim was put in Shallum's (Jehoahaz') stead by Pharaoh-necho. Jeconiah, his son, succeeded. Zedekiah (Mattaniah), uncle of Jeconiah, and brother of Jehoiakim and Jehoahaz, was last of all raised to the throne by Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen17928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He shall not return--</hi>The people perhaps entertained hopes of Shallum's return from Egypt, in which case they would replace him on the throne, and thereby free themselves from the oppressive taxes imposed by Jehoiakim. <div eID="gen17929" type="x-p"/>
entries.4eced03ad033c5e5919b2957381d81c035180627: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10061"/><div sID="gen17930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10061"/>13. Not only did Jehoiakim tax the people (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.35">2Ki 23:35</reference>) for Pharaoh's tribute, but also took their forced labor, without pay, for building a splendid palace; in violation of <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Le 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.14">De 24:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.15">15</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Mic.3.10">Mi 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.9">Ha 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jas 5:4</reference>. God will repay in justice those who will not in justice pay those whom they employ. <div eID="gen17930" type="x-p"/>
entries.7690f72df1241a909daf8b3f04f35638526fe08c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10062"/><div sID="gen17931" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10062"/><hi type="bold">14. wide--</hi>literally, "a house of dimensions" ("measures"). Compare <reference osisRef="Num.13.32">Nu 13:32</reference>, Margin, "men of statures."<div eID="gen17931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">large--</hi>rather, as Margin, "airy" from Hebrew root, "to breathe freely." Upper rooms in the East are the principal apartments.<div eID="gen17932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cutteth him out windows--</hi>The Hebrew, if a noun, is rather, "my windows"; then the translation ought to be, "and let my windows (Jehoiakim speaking) be cut out for it," that is, in the house; or, "and let (the workman) cut out my windows for it." But the word is rather an adjective; "he cutteth it (the house) out for himself, so as to be full of windows." The following words accord with this construction, "and (he makes it) ceiled with cedar," &c. [Maurer]. Retaining English Version, there must be understood something remarkable about the windows, since they are deemed worthy of notice. Gesenius thinks the word dual, "double windows," the blinds being two-leaved.<div eID="gen17933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vermilion--</hi>Hebrew, shashar, called so from a people of India beyond the Ganges, by whom it is exported [Pliny, 6.19]. The old vermilion was composed of sulphur and quicksilver; not of red lead, as our vermilion. <div eID="gen17934" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebdbd4ae559ade4cf859a2c17e07a13a7e21c46a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10063"/><div sID="gen17935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10063"/><hi type="bold">15. closest thyself--</hi>rather, "thou viest," that is, art emulous to surpass thy forefathers in the magnificence of thy palaces.<div eID="gen17935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat and drink--</hi>Did not Josiah, thy father, enjoy all that man really needs for his bodily wants? Did he need to build costly palaces to secure his throne? Nay, he did secure it by "judgment and justice"; whereas thou, with all thy luxurious building, sittest on a tottering throne.<div eID="gen17936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>on that account, therefore. <div eID="gen17937" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9f8a30fd62c991ac503d439ad1f65031dae8d07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10064"/><div sID="gen17938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10064"/><hi type="bold">16. was not this to know me--</hi>namely, to show by deeds that one knows God's will, as was the case with Josiah (compare <reference osisRef="John.13.17">Joh 13:17</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">Tit 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17938" type="x-p"/>
entries.545d63f0ad1e80047776e778faef25920b613db4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10065"/><div sID="gen17939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10065"/><hi type="bold">17. thine--</hi>as opposed to thy father, Josiah. <div eID="gen17939" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8ae3f1e1eec533fdcef4aa1bfe2088befd6f876: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10066"/><div sID="gen17940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10066"/><hi type="bold">18. Ah my brother! ... sister!--</hi>addressing him with such titles of affection as one would address to a deceased friend beloved as a brother or sister (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.30">1Ki 13:30</reference>). This expresses, They shall not lament him with the lamentation of private individuals [Vatablus], or of blood relatives [Grotius]: as "Ah! lord," expresses public lamentation in the case of a king [Vatablus], or that of subjects [Grotius]. Henderson thinks, "Ah! sister," refers to Jehoiakim's queen, who, though taken to Babylon and not left unburied on the way, as Jehoiakim, yet was not honored at her death with royal lamentations, such as would have been poured forth over her at Jerusalem. He notices the beauty of Jeremiah's manner in his prophecy against Jehoiakim. In <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.14">14</reference> he describes him in general terms; then, in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.17">Jr 22:15-17</reference>, he directly addresses him without naming him; at last, in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jr 22:18</reference>, he names him, but in the third person, to imply that God puts him to a distance from Him. The boldness of the Hebrew prophets proves their divine mission; were it not so, their reproofs to the Hebrew kings, who held the throne by divine authority, would have been treason.<div eID="gen17940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ah his glory!--</hi>"Alas! his majesty." <div eID="gen17941" type="x-p"/>
entries.64770954476fdbb800521fd070d8f350a7e36087: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10067"/><div sID="gen17942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10067"/><hi type="bold">19. burial of an ass--</hi>that is, he shall have the same burial as an ass would get, namely, he shall be left a prey for beasts and birds [Jerome]. This is not formally narrated. But <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference> states that "Nebuchadnezzar bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon"; his treatment there is nowhere mentioned. The prophecy here, and in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.30">Jr 36:30</reference>, harmonizes these two facts. He was slain by Nebuchadnezzar, who changed his purpose of taking him to Babylon, on the way thither, and left him unburied outside Jerusalem. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.6">2Ki 24:6</reference>, "Jehoiakim slept with his fathers," does not contradict this; it simply expresses his being gathered to his fathers by death, not his being buried with his fathers (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.19">Psa 49:19</reference>). The two phrases are found together, as expressing two distinct ideas (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.38">2Ki 15:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.20">16:20</reference>). <div eID="gen17942" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5eaf2c756e1e57889ebf9ccd17c1c842805b2d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10068"/><div sID="gen17943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10068"/>20. Delivered in the reign of Jehoiachin (Jeconiah or Coniah), son of Jehoiakim; appended to the previous prophecy respecting Jehoiakim, on account of the similarity of the two prophecies. He calls on Jerusalem, personified as a mourning female, to go up to the highest points visible from Jerusalem, and lament there (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.3.21">Jr 3:21</reference>) the calamity of herself, bereft of allies and of her princes, who are one after the other being cast down.<div eID="gen17943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bashan--</hi>north of the region beyond Jordan; the mountains of Anti-libanus are referred to (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.15">Psa 68:15</reference>).<div eID="gen17944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the passages--</hi>namely, of the rivers (<reference osisRef="Judg.12.6">Jud 12:6</reference>); or else the borders of the country (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.23">1Sa 13:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.29">Is 10:29</reference>). The passes (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1Sa 14:4</reference>). Maurer translates, "Abarim," a mountainous tract beyond Jordan, opposite Jericho, and south of Bashan; this accords with the mention of the mountains Lebanon and Bashan (<reference osisRef="Num.27.12">Nu 27:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.33.47">33:47</reference>).<div eID="gen17945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lovers--</hi>the allies of Judea, especially Egypt, now unable to help the Jews, being crippled by Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>). <div eID="gen17946" type="x-p"/>
entries.72170f6c4732167b47ce352267c31656bd8dfd0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10069"/><div sID="gen17947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10069"/>21. I admonished thee in time. Thy sin has not been a sin of ignorance or thoughtlessness, but wilful.<div eID="gen17947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prosperity--</hi>given thee by Me; yet thou wouldest not hearken to the gracious Giver. The Hebrew is plural, to express, "In the height of thy prosperity"; so "droughts" (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Is 58:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou saidst--</hi>not in words, but in thy conduct, virtually.<div eID="gen17949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy youth--</hi>from the time that I brought thee out of Egypt, and formed thee into a people (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.25">Jr 7:25</reference>; 2:2; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12">Is 47:12</reference>). <div eID="gen17950" type="x-p"/>
entries.72dbeb46efff87455ef4ae4e4f2baeea32cec112: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10070"/><div sID="gen17951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10070"/><hi type="bold">22. wind--</hi>the Chaldees, as a parching wind that sweeps over rapidly and withers vegetation (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.11">Jr 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Is 40:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat up ... pastors--</hi>that is, thy kings (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.8">Jr 2:8</reference>). There is a happy play on words. The pastors, whose office it is to feed the sheep, shall themselves be fed on. They who should drive the flock from place to place for pasture shall be driven into exile by the Chaldees. <div eID="gen17952" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cc574c0ae62d320cb1282d5211591eedfc47056: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10071"/><div sID="gen17953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10071"/><hi type="bold">23. inhabitant of Lebanon--</hi>namely, Jerusalem, whose temple, palaces, and principal habitations were built of cedars of Lebanon.<div eID="gen17953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how gracious--</hi>irony. How graciously thou wilt be treated by the Chaldees, when they come on thee suddenly, as pangs on a woman in travail (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.24">Jr 6:24</reference>)! Nay, all thy fine buildings will win no favor for thee from them. Maurer translates, "How shalt thou be to be pitied!" <div eID="gen17954" type="x-p"/>
entries.901baddc5808d7495f6185681ccbc7343a81eb4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10072"/><div sID="gen17955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10072"/><hi type="bold">24. As I live--</hi>God's most solemn formula of oath (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.18">Jr 46:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.2">4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.40">De 32:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.34">1Sa 25:34</reference>).<div eID="gen17955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Coniah--</hi>Jeconiah or Jehoiachin. The contraction of the name is meant in contempt.<div eID="gen17956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">signet--</hi>Such ring seals were often of the greatest value (<reference osisRef="Song.8.6">So 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.23">Hag 2:23</reference>). Jehoiachin's popularity is probably here referred to.<div eID="gen17957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right hand--</hi>the hand most valued.<div eID="gen17958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I would pluck thee thence--</hi>(Compare Ob 4); on account of thy father's sins, as well as thine own (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.9">2Ch 36:9</reference>). There is a change here, as often in Hebrew poetry, from the third to the second person, to bring the threat more directly home to him. After a three months' and ten days' reign, the Chaldees deposed him. In Babylon, however, by God's favor he was ultimately treated more kindly than other royal captives (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34">Jr 52:31-34</reference>). But none of his direct posterity ever came to the throne. <div eID="gen17959" type="x-p"/>
entries.20f2a0dd2ca76b1831d285ba1e6375e3785858d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10073"/><div sID="gen17960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10073"/><hi type="bold">25. give ... into ... hand--</hi>"I will pluck thee" from "my right hand," and "will give thee into the hand of them that seek thy life." <div eID="gen17960" type="x-p"/>
entries.1299c74d3a001ec7e563b11bdf830a48d78bdc93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10074"/><div sID="gen17961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10074"/><hi type="bold">26. thy mother--</hi>Nehushta, the queen dowager (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.6">2Ki 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.15">8, 15</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Jer.13.18">Jr 13:18</reference>). <div eID="gen17961" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fa7bd6e0f1a1d28727b8e5113c890e000123467: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10075"/><div sID="gen17962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10075"/><hi type="bold">27. they--</hi>Coniah and his mother. He passes from the second person (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.26">Jr 22:26</reference>) to the third person here, to express alienation. The king is as it were put out of sight, as if unworthy of being spoken with directly.<div eID="gen17962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desire--</hi>literally, "lift up their soul" (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">Jr 44:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">25:1</reference>). Judea was the land which they in Babylon should pine after in vain. <div eID="gen17963" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cb9bc5505a1593e1672e99025f7bf00a0fbb1c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10076"/><div sID="gen17964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10076"/><hi type="bold">28. broken idol--</hi>Coniah was idolized once by the Jews; Jeremiah, therefore, in their person, expresses their astonishment at one from whom so much had been expected being now so utterly cast aside.<div eID="gen17964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vessel ... no pleasure--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">Ho 8:8</reference>). The answer to this is given (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.20-Rom.9.23">Ro 9:20-23</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.21">2Ti 2:21</reference>).<div eID="gen17965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his seed--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.22.29">Jr 22:29</reference>). <div eID="gen17966" type="x-p"/>
entries.b727876a7263b2d2d1aff1488a5e773f66b2b0ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10077"/><div sID="gen17967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10077"/><hi type="bold">29-30. O earth! earth! earth!--</hi>Jeconiah was not actually without offspring (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jr 22:28</reference>, "his seed"; <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.17">1Ch 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.1.12">Mt 1:12</reference>), but he was to be "written childless," as a warning to posterity, that is, without a lineal heir to his throne. It is with a reference to the three kings, Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah, that the earth is thrice invoked [Bengel]. Or, the triple invocation is to give intensity to the call for attention to the announcement of the end of the royal line, so far as Jehoiachin's seed is concerned. Though Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.1-Matt.1.17">Mt 1:1-17</reference>), the heir of David's throne, was lineally descended from Jeconiah, it was only through Joseph, who, though His legal, was not His real father. Matthew gives the legal pedigree through Solomon down to Joseph; Luke the real pedigree, from Mary, the real parent, through Nathan, brother of Solomon, upwards (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.31">Lu 3:31</reference>).<div eID="gen17967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man of his seed ... upon the throne--</hi>This explains the sense in which "childless" is used. Though the succession to the throne failed in his line, still the promise to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.37">Psa 89:30-37</reference>) was revived in Zerubbabel and consummated in Christ. <chapter eID="Jer.22"/>

entries.b09f79d0b665ec1b61a86b0d9b68525d9ef4bfe8: <div eID="gen29836" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29837" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29838" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29838" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29837" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29839" type="x-p"/> This section of prophecy, extending to the end of the eighth verse of the next chapter, is addressed to the king of Judah and his people. It enjoins on them the practice of justice and equity, as they would hope to prosper, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.14">Jer 22:14</reference>; but threatens them, in case of disobedience, with utter destruction, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.5-Jer.22.9">Jer 22:5-9</reference>. The captivity of Shallum, the son of Josiah, is declared to be irreversible, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.10-Jer.22.12">Jer 22:10-12</reference>; and the miserable and unlamented end of Jeconiah, contemptuously called Coniah, is foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.19">Jer 22:13-19</reference>. His family is threatened with the like captivity, and his seed declared to be for ever excluded from the throne, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.20-Jer.22.30">Jer 22:20-30</reference>. <div eID="gen29839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29840" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29841" type="x-p"/> Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak there this word - This is supposed by Dahler to have been published in the first year of the reign of Zedekiah.
entries.66fbfd8a0c50ff6a25dca11b9e9d8bd0d17a4fc4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29842" type="x-p"/> O king of Judah - thou, and thy servants - His ministers are here addressed, as chiefly governing the nation; and who had counselled Zedekiah to rebel.
